t1: Write a Python function `def compare_versions(a: str, b: str) -> int` that returns -1 if version a is lower than version b, 0 if they are equal, and 1 if a is higher. A version is a core of one or more dot-separated non-negative integers (like `1.2.10`), optionally followed by `-` and a pre-release part made of dot-separated identifiers (like `1.0.0-beta.2`). Compare cores numerically component by component, treating missing trailing components as 0, so `1.2` equals `1.2.0`. If the cores are equal, a version without a pre-release part is higher than one with a pre-release part. Two pre-release parts are compared identifier by identifier from the left: two purely numeric identifiers compare as numbers, two non-numeric identifiers compare by ASCII string order, and a numeric identifier is always lower than a non-numeric one. If every compared identifier is equal, the part with fewer identifiers is lower.
t2: Also accept an optional leading `v` or `V` (like `v1.2`), and an optional build part: `+` followed by dot-separated identifiers, after the core or the pre-release part (like `1.0.0-rc.1+build.5`); split it off at the first `+`. The build part only matters when two versions are otherwise equal: then a version without a build part is lower than one with it, and two build parts are compared with the same rules as pre-release parts.
t3: Change how two non-numeric identifiers compare, in both pre-release and build parts: split each into its leading non-digit part and its trailing run of digits (the digit run may be empty, as in `beta`). Compare the leading parts by ASCII order first, then the digit runs as numbers, with an empty digit run lower than any number. So `rc2` < `rc10` and `rc` < `rc0`. You can assume every non-numeric identifier has this shape.
tests:
def test_core_numeric_and_padding():
    assert compare_versions("1.2", "1.2.0") == 0
    assert compare_versions("1.2.0.0", "1.2") == 0
    assert compare_versions("1.2.10", "1.2.9") == 1
    assert compare_versions("1.10", "1.9.9") == 1
    assert compare_versions("2", "10") == -1
    assert compare_versions("1.02", "1.2") == 0
    assert compare_versions("1.2", "1.2.1") == -1


def test_prerelease_below_release():
    assert compare_versions("1.2.0-rc.1", "1.2") == -1
    assert compare_versions("1.2", "1.2.0-alpha") == 1
    assert compare_versions("1.2.1-alpha", "1.2") == 1


def test_prerelease_identifier_rules():
    assert compare_versions("1.0.0-2", "1.0.0-10") == -1
    assert compare_versions("1.0.0-99", "1.0.0-a") == -1
    assert compare_versions("1.0.0-alpha", "1.0.0-alpha.1") == -1
    assert compare_versions("1.0.0-alpha.beta", "1.0.0-alpha.1") == 1
    assert compare_versions("1.0.0-Beta", "1.0.0-alpha") == -1
    assert compare_versions("1.0.0-alpha.1", "1.0.0-alpha.1") == 0


def test_v_prefix():
    assert compare_versions("v1.0", "1.0.0") == 0
    assert compare_versions("V2.0.0-rc.1", "2.0.0-rc.1") == 0
    assert compare_versions("v1.0.1", "1.0.0") == 1


def test_build_part_is_only_a_final_tie_break():
    assert compare_versions("1.0.0+1", "1.0") == 1
    assert compare_versions("v1.0+build.7", "1.0.0") == 1
    assert compare_versions("1.0.0-rc.1+zzz", "1.0.0-rc.2") == -1
    assert compare_versions("1.0.1", "1.0.0+999") == 1
    assert compare_versions("1.0-rc+x", "1.0-rc") == 1
    assert compare_versions("1.0-rc+x", "1.0") == -1
    assert compare_versions("1.0.0+exp-sha.5", "1.0+exp-sha.5") == 0


def test_build_parts_compare_like_prerelease_parts():
    assert compare_versions("1.0.0+b.2", "1.0.0+b.10") == -1
    assert compare_versions("1.0+5", "1.0+a") == -1
    assert compare_versions("1.0+a", "1.0+a.1") == -1
    assert compare_versions("1.0+B", "1.0+a") == -1
    assert compare_versions("1.0.0+zzz", "1.0.0+aaa") == 1


def test_letters_then_digits_identifiers():
    assert compare_versions("1.0.0-rc2", "1.0.0-rc10") == -1
    assert compare_versions("1.0.0-rc10", "1.0.0-rc2") == 1
    assert compare_versions("1.0.0-rc", "1.0.0-rc0") == -1
    assert compare_versions("1.0.0-beta10", "1.0.0-rc1") == -1
    assert compare_versions("1.0.0-rc01", "1.0.0-rc1") == 0
    assert compare_versions("1.0.0-rc.1", "1.0.0-rc1") == -1
    assert compare_versions("1.0+x2", "1.0+x10") == -1
    assert compare_versions("1.0+build", "1.0+build0") == -1


def test_combined_rules():
    assert compare_versions("v1.2-rc.3", "1.2.0-rc.3+x") == -1
    assert compare_versions("1.2-alpha10.2", "1.2.0-alpha9.10") == 1
    assert compare_versions("1.0.0-7", "1.0.0-rc") == -1
    assert compare_versions("1.0-rc2.beta", "1.0-rc2.alpha3") == 1
    assert compare_versions("V3-rc9+b10", "3.0.0-rc9+b9") == 1

Mutants: no core padding, '-' split before '+', build ignored (semver prior), T3 ignored, T3 only for pre-release, empty digit run as 0, numeric/non-numeric flipped, fewer-identifiers rule flipped.

t1: Write a Python function `def wrap_text(text: str, width: int) -> list` that word-wraps text and returns the lines as a list of strings. Words are maximal runs of non-whitespace characters; any whitespace (spaces, tabs, newlines) only separates words. Fill lines greedily: add each word to the current line, separated by a single space, if the line's length stays <= width; otherwise start a new line with it. A word longer than width is broken: it starts on a fresh line (unless the current line is still empty) and is cut into chunks of exactly width characters, the last chunk possibly shorter; that last chunk then acts like a normal word, so following words may join its line. Lines never have leading or trailing spaces. Return [] if the text has no words. Assume width >= 1.
t2: Now support paragraphs: a line of the input that is empty or whitespace-only separates paragraphs (several such lines in a row count as one separator, and separators at the very start or end are ignored). Wrap each paragraph on its own and put exactly one empty string between consecutive paragraphs in the output. Also, when the previous word on a line ends with `.`, `!` or `?`, the separator before the next word on that line is two spaces instead of one (both count toward the width).
t3: Change the long-word rule: if the current line already has text, first add the usual separator and as many leading characters of the long word as still fit on that line, but only if at least 2 characters fit; otherwise start a fresh line as before. Whatever remains of the word is then cut into width-sized chunks as before.
tests:
def test_greedy_fill_with_inclusive_width():
    assert wrap_text("the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog", 10) == [
        "the quick", "brown fox", "jumps over", "the lazy", "dog"]


def test_whitespace_and_empty_input():
    assert wrap_text("  a\tb\n c  ", 5) == ["a b c"]
    assert wrap_text("one\ntwo", 7) == ["one two"]
    assert wrap_text("", 5) == []
    assert wrap_text(" \n\t\n ", 5) == []


def test_long_word_on_empty_line_and_last_chunk_joins():

    assert wrap_text("abcdefghij x", 4) == ["abcd", "efgh", "ij x"]
    assert wrap_text("abcdef", 6) == ["abcdef"]
    assert wrap_text("ab abcdef", 6) == ["ab", "abcdef"]


def test_paragraphs():

    assert wrap_text("\n\nhello\n\n", 10) == ["hello"]

    assert wrap_text("Stop! go", 9) == ["Stop!  go"]
    assert wrap_text("e.g. x? y", 20) == ["e.g.  x?  y"]
    assert wrap_text("a.b c", 10) == ["a.b c"]
    assert wrap_text("one. two three", 9) == ["one.  two", "three"]

    assert wrap_text("abc defghijk", 6) == ["abc de", "fghijk"]

    assert wrap_text("abcde fghijklm", 6) == ["abcde", "fghijk", "lm"]


def test_long_words_with_sentence_spacing():

def test_paragraphs_with_long_words():

t1: Write a Python function `def render(template: str, values: dict) -> str` that fills placeholders in a template string. A placeholder is `{name}`, where name matches `[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*`; it is replaced by `str(values[name])`. `{{` produces a literal `{` and `}}` produces a literal `}`. If a placeholder's name is not a key of values, raise KeyError. Any other brace use — a `{` that doesn't start `{{` or a valid placeholder, or a lone `}` — raises ValueError. The template is scanned left to right and each piece is consumed as it is recognised, so in `{{{x}}}` the first two braces give a literal `{`, then `{x}` is a placeholder, then `}}` gives a literal `}`.
t2: Add defaults: `{name|fallback}` renders the fallback text when name is missing from values (if name is present, its value is used, whatever it is). The fallback is everything between the first `|` and the next `}`, may be empty, and is inserted literally; if it contains a `{`, raise ValueError.
t3: Also support dotted names like `{user.name}` and `{items.0}`: the first part must be a valid name, and each later part must be a valid name or a run of digits without leading zeros (`0` itself is fine). The lookup walks the value one part at a time: on a dict, the part (digits included) is looked up as a string key; on a list, a digits part is used as an index (`values['items'][0]`). If any step fails — a missing key, an index out of range, or a value of any other type, including a non-digit part on a list — the placeholder counts as missing (KeyError, or the fallback if one is given).
tests:
import pytest


def test_basic_substitution():
    assert render("Hi {name}, you are {age}.", {"name": "Bo", "age": 7}) == "Hi Bo, you are 7."
    assert render("{a}{a}{_b2}", {"a": "x", "_b2": [1]}) == "xx[1]"
    assert render("no placeholders", {}) == "no placeholders"


def test_brace_escapes_scan_left_to_right():
    assert render("{{x}} {{{x}}}", {"x": 1}) == "{x} {1}"
    assert render("}}{{", {}) == "}{"


def test_syntax_errors_and_missing_keys():
    for bad in ["{", "a}b", "{1x}", "{}", "{a}}", "{a b}", "{a", "}}}"]:
        with pytest.raises(ValueError):
            render(bad, {"a": 1})
    with pytest.raises(KeyError):
        render("{zz}", {"a": 1})


def test_fallbacks():
    assert render("{a|none} {b|} {c|x|y}", {"b": 0}) == "none 0 x|y"
    assert render("{a|hello world}!", {}) == "hello world!"
    assert render("{a|}", {}) == ""
    assert render("{a|x}", {"a": None}) == "None"
    assert render("{a|x}", {"a": ""}) == ""
    assert render("{{{a|b}}}", {}) == "{b}"


def test_fallback_syntax_errors():
    for bad in ["{a|x{y}", "{a b|x}", "{|x}", "{a|x"]:
        with pytest.raises(ValueError):
            render(bad, {})


def test_dotted_lookup():
    data = {"u": {"name": "Al", "addr": "n/a", "tags": {"k": 3}}}
    assert render("{u.name} {u.tags.k}", data) == "Al 3"
    assert render("{u.addr.city|?}", data) == "?"
    assert render("{u.zip|-}", data) == "-"
    with pytest.raises(KeyError):
        render("{u.zip}", data)
    with pytest.raises(KeyError):
        render("{u.addr.city}", data)
    with pytest.raises(KeyError):
        render("{a.b}", {"a.b": 1})


def test_dotted_syntax_errors():
    for bad in ["{u.}", "{.u}", "{u..v}", "{u.|x}", "{u.v w}"]:
        with pytest.raises(ValueError):
            render(bad, {"u": {"v": 1}})


def test_list_indexing():
    data = {"items": [7, {"name": "x"}], "m": {"0": "zero"}, "s": "abc", "t": (1,)}
    assert render("{items.0}-{items.1.name}", data) == "7-x"
    assert render("{items.2|none}", data) == "none"
    assert render("{m.0}", data) == "zero"
    assert render("{s.0|?}", data) == "?"
    assert render("{items.name|?}", data) == "?"
    assert render("{t.0|tuple}", data) == "tuple"
    with pytest.raises(KeyError):
        render("{items.5}", data)
    with pytest.raises(KeyError):
        render("{m.1}", data)


def test_index_syntax_errors():
    for bad in ["{items.01}", "{items.-1}", "{0}", "{0.a}", "{items.1a}", "{items.0x1}"]:
        with pytest.raises(ValueError):
            render(bad, {"items": [1, 2]})
notes: Left-to-right brace scanning (e.g. `{a}}` is an error, `{{{x}}}` is fine), a fallback that must be used only when the key is absent (not when falsy), first-'|' splitting, and nested lookup over dicts and lists (digit parts index lists but are string keys on dicts; tuples, strings, out-of-range and flat dotted keys count as missing). Mutants: falsy-value fallback, rsplit on '|', flat-key-first lookup, try/except lookup that leaks ValueError/TypeError, replace-escapes-then-regex approach, leading-zero indexes accepted, tuples indexed, digit parts converted to int on dicts.

t1: Write a Python function `def normalize_path(path: str) -> str` that normalizes a POSIX-style path purely as text (no filesystem access). Split the path on `/`. Drop empty segments and `.` segments. A `..` segment removes the most recent kept segment, if there is one and it isn't itself `..`; otherwise, in a relative path the `..` is kept, and in an absolute path (one starting with `/`) it would climb above the root, so raise ValueError. A segment made only of k >= 3 dots counts as k - 1 `..` segments in a row (so `...` means `../..`). An absolute path's result starts with `/`; a relative path that normalizes to nothing becomes `.`. The result never ends with `/` unless it is exactly `/`. Every other segment, like `..a` or `.b.`, is an ordinary name.
t2: Add home expansion via a new parameter, making the signature `def normalize_path(path: str, home: str = '/home/user') -> str`: if the path is exactly `~` or starts with `~/`, replace that `~` with home before normalizing, and normalize the combined path as a whole (home may contain things like `//` or a trailing `/`; assume it is absolute). A `~` anywhere else, or one followed by other characters as in `~bob`, is an ordinary name.
t3: I think your `..` handling double-counts in relative paths: `normalize_path('x/y/../../../z')` returns `'../z'`, but x and y should absorb the `..` segments, so it looks like a `..` is being kept after it already cancelled a segment. Please fix that.

import pytest


def test_absolute_paths():
    assert normalize_path("/a/./b//c/") == "/a/b/c"
    assert normalize_path("/") == "/"
    assert normalize_path("///") == "/"
    assert normalize_path("/a/..") == "/"
    assert normalize_path("/a/b/../../c") == "/c"


def test_absolute_path_cannot_climb_above_root():
    for bad in ["/..", "/../a", "/a/../..", "/a/b/../../../c"]:
        with pytest.raises(ValueError):
            normalize_path(bad)


def test_relative_paths_keep_unmatched_dotdot():
    assert normalize_path("a/b/../c") == "a/c"
    assert normalize_path("a/../../b") == "../b"
    assert normalize_path("x/y/../../../z") == "../z"
    assert normalize_path("../../x/..") == "../.."
    assert normalize_path("../a/../..") == "../.."


def test_relative_empty_and_dots():
    assert normalize_path("a/..") == "."
    assert normalize_path("./") == "."
    assert normalize_path("") == "."
    assert normalize_path("a//b/./") == "a/b"
    assert normalize_path("..a/b") == "..a/b"
    assert normalize_path("a/.b./c") == "a/.b./c"


def test_multi_dot_segments():
    assert normalize_path("a/b/c/...") == "a"
    assert normalize_path("a/...") == ".."
    assert normalize_path("x/....") == "../.."
    assert normalize_path(".../a") == "../../a"
    assert normalize_path("a/.../b/..") == ".."
    assert normalize_path("/a/b/...") == "/"
    with pytest.raises(ValueError):
        normalize_path("/a/...")


def test_home_expansion():
    assert normalize_path("~") == "/home/user"
    assert normalize_path("~/") == "/home/user"
    assert normalize_path("~/docs/../x") == "/home/user/x"
    assert normalize_path("~/...") == "/"
    assert normalize_path("~/x", home="/srv//me/") == "/srv/me/x"
    with pytest.raises(ValueError):
        normalize_path("~/../../..")
    with pytest.raises(ValueError):
        normalize_path("~/..", home="/")


def test_tilde_elsewhere_is_an_ordinary_name():
    assert normalize_path("~bob/x") == "~bob/x"
    assert normalize_path("a/~/b") == "a/~/b"
    assert normalize_path("/~/a") == "/~/a"
    assert normalize_path("./~") == "~"

t1: Write a Python function `def filter_records(records: list, query: str) -> list` that returns the records (dicts) matching a query string, in their original order. A query is one or more conditions joined by the keywords `and` / `or`, where `and` binds tighter than `or`. A condition is `field op value`: field is a name of letters, digits and underscores not starting with a digit; op is one of `=`, `!=`, `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`; value is an integer literal (digits, optionally with a `-` directly in front) or a double-quoted string. Whitespace between tokens is optional (`age>=30` is fine). A condition is false if the record lacks the field, or if the record's value and the literal are not both int or both str (a bool counts as neither); otherwise compare them normally. Raise ValueError for any malformed query.

    {"name": "cy"},

    assert names(filter_records(PEOPLE, "age!=31")) == ["bob", "Eve"]
    assert names(filter_records(PEOPLE, 'name < "b"')) == ["ann", "Eve"]
    assert names(filter_records(PEOPLE, "vip = 1")) == []
    assert names(filter_records(PEOPLE, "age > -5 and age<26")) == ["bob"]

    assert names(filter_records(PEOPLE, 'age = 40 or age = 25 and name = "bob" or name = "cy"')) == ["bob", "cy", "Eve"]


def test_malformed_queries_raise_even_with_no_records():

    assert names(filter_records(PEOPLE, "not age = 31")) == ["bob", "cy", "dee", "Eve"]
    assert names(filter_records(PEOPLE, 'not age = 31 and name != "cy"')) == ["bob", "dee", "Eve"]
    assert names(filter_records(PEOPLE, "not (age = 25 or age = 31)")) == ["cy", "dee", "Eve"]
    assert names(filter_records(PEOPLE, "not not age = 25")) == ["bob"]
    assert names(filter_records(PEOPLE, "((age>30))")) == ["ann", "Eve"]

def test_field_names_that_start_with_keywords():

t1: Write a Python function `def split_command(line: str) -> list` that splits a command line into a list of arguments, shell-style. Unquoted spaces and tabs separate arguments (runs of them count as one; leading and trailing ones are ignored). Text inside single quotes is taken literally, with no escapes. Inside double quotes, a backslash followed by `"`, `\` or `$` produces that character, and any other backslash is kept as a literal backslash. Outside quotes, a backslash makes the next character literal (including a space or a quote). Quoted and unquoted pieces that touch form one argument (`a"b c"'d'` gives `ab cd`), and `""` or `''` on its own gives an empty argument. Raise ValueError for an unterminated quote or a backslash at the very end of the line.
t2: Add variable expansion with a new parameter, making the signature `def split_command(line: str, env: dict = None) -> list` (None means an empty dict). `$NAME` or `${NAME}`, where NAME is a letter or `_` followed by letters, digits or `_` (as many as possible), is replaced by `env.get(NAME, '')`, both outside quotes and inside double quotes, but not inside single quotes or when the `$` is escaped. A `$` not followed by a valid name start or `{` is a literal `$`; a `${` not followed by a valid name and `}` raises ValueError. Expanded text is never split on spaces.
t3: One more rule: an argument that comes out empty and was built only from unquoted variable expansions is dropped entirely, so `a $X b` with X unset gives `['a', 'b']`; arguments with any quoted part, like `"$X"` or `$X''`, are kept even if empty. Also support `${NAME:-default}`: it expands to NAME's value, or to default when NAME is missing from env or maps to an empty string, where default is the literal text up to the next `}` (no escapes or expansions inside it, and like any expansion it is not split on spaces). It counts as a variable expansion for the dropping rule.

ENV = {"HOME": "/home/me", "E": "", "SP": "a b", "X1": "v"}

    assert split_command("   ") == []
    assert split_command("echo 'a  b' \"c d\"") == ["echo", "a  b", "c d"]
    assert split_command("a\"b c\"'d'") == ["ab cd"]
    assert split_command("'' \"\" x") == ["", "", "x"]

    assert split_command(r'"a\"b" "c\\d" "e\f"') == ['a"b', "c\\d", "e\\f"]
    assert split_command(r"'it\'") == ["it\\"]
    assert split_command(r"\\") == ["\\"]

        with pytest.raises(ValueError):
            split_command(bad)

    assert split_command("\"$HOME\" '$HOME' \\$HOME \"\\$HOME\"", ENV) == ["/home/me", "$HOME", "$HOME", "$HOME"]
    assert split_command("a$X1.b ${X1}y", ENV) == ["av.b", "vy"]
    assert split_command("x $SP y", ENV) == ["x", "a b", "y"]
    assert split_command("\"[$SP]\"", ENV) == ["[a b]"]


def test_lone_dollar_is_literal():
    assert split_command("$ $1 a$ $-x \"$\"", ENV) == ["$", "$1", "a$", "$-x", "$"]


def test_bad_brace_expansions():
    for bad in ["${", "${}", "${1A}", "${A", "\"${A\"", "${A B}"]:
        with pytest.raises(ValueError):
            split_command(bad, ENV)


def test_empty_unquoted_expansions_are_dropped():
    assert split_command("a $NOPE b", ENV) == ["a", "b"]
    assert split_command("$E$NOPE ${E}", ENV) == []
    assert split_command("\"$NOPE\" $E'' x$E", ENV) == ["", "", "x"]
    assert split_command("$NOPE$X1 \\$E", ENV) == ["v", "$E"]
    assert split_command("echo $HOME") == ["echo"]


def test_default_values():
    assert split_command("${NOPE:-x y} ${HOME:-z}", ENV) == ["x y", "/home/me"]
    assert split_command("${E:-dflt} ${E:-}", ENV) == ["dflt"]
    assert split_command("\"${NOPE:-}\" ${X1:-q}", ENV) == ["", "v"]
    assert split_command("${NOPE:-$HOME}x '${NOPE:-q}'", ENV) == ["$HOMEx", "${NOPE:-q}"]
